opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think those two ideas are really two sides of the same coin when you're thinking about an agent that has to come to understand a world it wasn't born knowing.

Start with iterative refinement. When you or I approach a new problem, whether it's writing a piece of code, figuring out how some physical system works, or learning a new game, we almost never get it right on the first shot. We make a guess, we try it, we see where it breaks, and then we revise. That loop of propose, test, and fix is incredibly powerful, because it means you don't need to search the entire space of possible solutions blindly. You get feedback from the world, and the feedback tells you where to look next. A lot of classical program synthesis treated the problem as a one-shot search: here's a spec, find the program. But real intelligence looks much more like debugging. You have a hypothesis that's mostly right, and you're incrementally repairing it. And especially now that we have language models that can propose reasonable first drafts, the bottleneck becomes how you refine those drafts efficiently, how you decide which hypothesis to keep working on versus which to throw away.

Compositional knowledge is what makes that refinement scale. If every time you learned something new it was a monolithic blob, you'd have to relearn everything from scratch for each new task. But if what you learn is broken into reusable pieces, little abstractions, little subroutines, little concepts, then the next problem you face is easier because you can build on what you already have. That's a big part of what we were after with work like DreamCoder: the system solves some problems, notices recurring structure in its solutions, pulls that structure out into a library, and then that library makes the next round of problems tractable. You get this snowball effect where the agent's vocabulary for thinking about the world grows over time.

And the two interact. Refinement gives you the solutions, and compression into compositional pieces turns those solutions into knowledge. Then that knowledge makes your future refinements faster and more targeted, because you're editing in a much richer language. So for an agent interacting with the world, say building a world model in some environment, you want it to form theories, test them against what it observes, repair them when they fail, and crucially, keep the parts that worked in a form it can reuse. That's what lets it generalize from a handful of experiences rather than needing millions of examples. I think that's one of the most important gaps between how humans learn and how most current systems learn, and these two ingredients go a long way toward closing it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it comes from looking at what humans actually do when they encounter something new, and noticing how different it is from the standard picture of learning that we work with in machine learning.

So the standard picture is: you get a big pile of data, you fit a function to it, and if you want the function to get better, you give it more data or more parameters. And that's been enormously successful, I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But when you watch a person, or a kid, or even a scientist, interact with some new system, that's not what they're doing. They form a theory, a hypothesis about how the thing works, they poke at it, the thing does something they didn't expect, and then they don't throw the theory away and start over. They patch it. They say, okay, most of what I believed is still right, but this one piece needs to change. That's iterative refinement. And it's incredibly data efficient, because every revision is reusing almost all of what came before.

Now, the reason compositionality matters is that it's what makes that patching possible. If your knowledge is just one big undifferentiated blob of weights, there's no "piece" to patch. You can't say "this part of my model is wrong" because there aren't parts. But if your model of the world is built out of components that fit together, so, like, a program, or a library of concepts, or a set of rules, then when something goes wrong you can localize the error. You can say, the physics was fine, but my assumption about this particular object was wrong. And then you fix that one thing and everything else keeps working.

And the other thing compositionality buys you is reuse. If I learn something in one environment and the knowledge is structured, I can carry pieces of it over to a new environment. I don't have to relearn that objects persist, or that gravity points down, every time the surface features change. The pieces recombine. That's kind of the whole point of having concepts rather than just reflexes.

So I'd say those two ideas really depend on each other. Compositional representations are what make iterative refinement tractable, and iterative refinement is how you actually grow a compositional library over time without having to get everything right on the first try. And the interesting research question, for me, is how you get that kind of learner out of the tools we have now. Because the big models are very good at proposing plausible hypotheses, they've seen a lot of programs, a lot of explanations. What they're less good at, out of the box, is the loop: proposing, testing against the world, noticing the discrepancy, and making a targeted revision. That loop is where I think a lot of the action is.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think they address two connected problems. One is that you’re almost never going to get your understanding of the world right on the first try. You take an action, you observe what happens, and you discover that some part of your model was wrong. So you need a way to revise what you believe—to treat a failed prediction as information that helps you construct a better explanation.

The other problem is that you can’t learn every situation independently. You need knowledge that you can reuse. If you’ve learned how to grasp something and how to move your hand to a location, you’d like to compose those capabilities to move an object, rather than learn that whole behavior from scratch.

And these reinforce each other. Having compositional knowledge gives you pieces you can revise individually. If a plan fails, perhaps the issue is your understanding of grasping, rather than the entire plan. And iterative refinement helps you discover which pieces are actually useful across situations.

The challenge is that you don’t know the right pieces in advance. So the agent needs to learn both how to solve particular problems and how to organize what it learns so that the next problem becomes easier.

r003.rationale: It says reusable capabilities can be composed, revised individually, and organized so each new problem becomes easier, conveying how compositional knowledge supports growth over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re closely connected. When an agent interacts with the world, it rarely gets everything right on the first attempt. It has to try something, observe what happens, and revise its understanding or its plan. Iterative refinement gives it a way to learn from that feedback instead of having to produce a perfect answer in one shot.

But you also want that learning to accumulate. If every new task requires starting from scratch, you’re throwing away a lot of experience. Compositional knowledge lets you take things you already understand—actions, concepts, little procedures—and combine them to solve a new problem.

Think about learning to write a program. You write something, run it, discover a mistake, and fix it. Over time, you also discover useful functions that you can reuse. Those functions make subsequent programs easier to write, and trying to write new programs reveals where your functions need to change. For an agent, I think that interaction is important: refining individual solutions while also building a reusable vocabulary that makes future learning easier.
